findings.text: Callers consult a mediation hook around each sensitive action across inode, file, mapping, task, credential, IPC, network, device, key, path and audit domains and proceed on a success indication. The fragments show the no-policy fallback shape where each hook carries no persistent decision state.

The dominant fallback contract is to allow. Permission, allocation, association, control, connection lifecycle, teardown and notification hooks report success or do nothing, so denial must come from another layer. Empty release and free paths imply no retained allocation needs cleanup here.

A small subset does not decide locally and forwards to the capability helper for the same operation. This covers inode privilege handling and attribute security retrieval, low address mapping, and selected task controls for identity fixup, priority, scheduling and control operations.

Negative and special outcomes are grouped by category. Attribute, context translation, labelled context, copy-up attribute and user context fill operations report an unsupported outcome. Process attribute access reports an invalid argument outcome. Peer security retrieval on stream and datagram sockets reports an unavailable protocol option outcome. Transform state against policy flow comparison reports an affirmative match rather than plain success.

Label and identity outputs start neutral. Inode, IPC and task label properties initialize to an empty value, credential identity reads as zero, and key security retrieval yields a null buffer with success. Label-name query reports false here, and lockdown and device integrity hooks report success.

The interface exposes lifecycle coverage for sockets, security associations and auxiliary transports, including creation, binding, connection, listening, acceptance, message transfer, option handling, shutdown, cloning, classification, grafting, request handling, marking, tunnel device handling, partition and subnet handling, association handling, subflow addition and transform policy and state handling.

No locking, ordering, sleeping, interrupt or concurrency contract is visible. Hooks take caller-owned objects and return directly without acquiring, releasing, asserting or documenting any lock, so no hierarchy or exclusion can be inferred from these fragments.

Treating these fallbacks as enforcement would be unsafe because they allow by default, retain no decision state, and provide empty teardown. Callers must still validate inputs, handle allocation failure elsewhere, and obtain real policy from another layer. Absence of checks here is a build-mode property, not a safety guarantee.

The observable outcome contract uses zero to mean allow or success, one to mean transform flow match, and distinct negative failures to separate unsupported operation from invalid argument and from unavailable protocol option. These are caller-visible branching facts, not policy decisions.
